summary:
Georgia is dangerous for trans visitors, and the position has deteriorated sharply. In September 2024 the Parliament of Georgia adopted the law "On the Protection of Family Values and Minors", which bans legal gender recognition, transition-related healthcare, public LGBT assembly and the dissemination of "LGBT information". It is the harshest such legislative package in the region, and it removed the two routes by which a trans visitor or resident would ordinarily deal with documents and care.

One day after the law passed, Kesaria Abramidze, a trans model and influencer and one of Georgia's best-known transgender women, was stabbed to death in her apartment in Tbilisi. German foreign-affairs committee chair Michael Roth and EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell condemned the law as further derailing Georgia's EU path. AP reported in October 2024 that the killing, together with Russia-style "gay propaganda" provisions, had raised fears of hate crimes against LGBT people in the conservative South Caucasus nation.

The refusal of protection by the security apparatus predates the 2024 law. In June 2019 the Interior Ministry declared the country's first-ever Tbilisi Pride "impossible" in the planned city-centre locations, citing safety risks; organisers reported a week of pressure from an unidentified government official to cancel the march, and far-right groups had vowed to thwart it. In 2021 the Pride office was ransacked by far-right mobs while police stood by, and investigators have documented police failure to protect demonstrators.

The machinery of protection is itself under strain. The foreign-agents law is choking local rights groups and LGBT organisations, which refuse to register as "foreign agents" and consequently face fines or bankruptcy. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records that the anti-LGBTI law has eroded trust in institutions, that applications to LGBTI services have fallen as a result, that large numbers of LGBTI people are fleeing Georgia and seeking asylum documentation, and that misinformation demonising the LGBTI community is spreading.

Trans-specific legal barriers are older than the 2024 package. Legal activists told IWPR in May 2012 that the law needed changing to allow gender recognition, and that job applications become difficult when a person's gender identity does not match official paperwork. In August 2024 WISG and partner organisations reported to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers calling for urgent action: effective investigations into anti-LGBTI violence, withdrawal of the proposed anti-LGBTI legislation, improved hate-crime data collection, and protection of LGBTI assembly and expression. Those requests describe protections that are not currently in force.
tangentialFactors:
The legislative package is widely read as an import of the Russian "gay propaganda" model, a comparison AP made explicitly in its October 2024 reporting; the parallel matters because that model has been used elsewhere as a gateway to broader restriction of assembly and expression rather than as an endpoint in itself.

The foreign-agents law follows the same template as equivalent legislation in other post-Soviet states, and its effect on civil society is measurable: organisations that refuse the "foreign agents" label lose registration and face fines or bankruptcy, which removes the domestic organisations that would otherwise document abuse.

Georgia's EU accession path provides an external pressure point. Condemnation from Michael Roth and Josep Borrell framed the anti-LGBTI law as a further derailment of that path, which gives foreign governments a stated interest in the regime but has not so far produced a reversal of the statute.

The Council of Europe route is open: a national LGBTI organisation filed an implementation report to the Committee of Measures in August 2024, so the country stands under review by a supranational human rights mechanism alongside its domestic courts.

The 2012 and 2019 episodes show the pattern is not recent or solely legislative. Document discrimination in employment paperwork, an interior ministry blocking a pride march on safety grounds, and street violence met with police inaction recur across more than a decade.
localsOnly:
Residents cannot obtain legal gender recognition under the 2024 law, so official documents continue to mismatch lived gender; the employment consequence identified as far back as 2012, in which job applications fail when paperwork does not match identity, now has a statutory basis rather than an administrative one.

Transition-related healthcare is banned, which removes domestic access to hormone therapy and surgical care for people already mid-course, and residents who continue treatment abroad do so without legal cover at home.

Service provision for LGBT residents has contracted. Organisations that decline to register under the foreign-agents law face fines and bankruptcy, and ILGA-Europe records a fall in service applications as trust in institutions declines, so fewer residents seek help even where it is still offered.

Residents, unlike short-term visitors, bear the long-term consequences of the information ban: public assembly is prohibited, and dissemination of "LGBT information" is a criminal matter, which affects teaching, publishing and online posting.

A large number of LGBT residents have left the country or are preparing documentation for asylum applications, and the misinformation circulating about the community has tangible effects on everyday safety, housing and employment.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the killing of Kesaria Abramidze has resulted in arrests, charges or convictions is not sourced in the available inventory; the reporting establishes the death and its timing against the law, not the criminal outcome.

The quality and completeness of hate-crime data collection is not resolved here. The August 2024 report to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers recommends improved collection, which implies gaps, but no figures on recorded anti-trans offences or prosecution rates are available in the inventory.

The enforcement posture of the 2024 law against visitors specifically is not documented. The inventory establishes the statutory bans and a documented pattern of police non-protection of demonstrators, but contains no reported case of a foreign visitor prosecuted under the package.

The status of the 2019 and 2021 incidents as to any legal liability of the Interior Ministry or of the mobs remains unresolved; no sourced outcome of investigations or litigation is available.

The 2012 employment-material is more than a decade old and predates both the 2024 statute and subsequent administrative changes, so its precise current application to residents is undated rather than confirmed.

The extent to which the foreign-agents law's registration requirements fall on a foreign visitor's own advocacy, as distinct on resident organisations, is not sourced and should be verified with a Georgian legal adviser before relying on it.
